## Four Results You Should Expect {.band-bottom}

| | |
|---|---|
| Two groups with identical scores | one of them flipped every sign |
| A group near +0.015 | that is the noise floor, not a small edge |
| A group at exactly 0.000 | constant predictions; no variance, no coefficient |
| A group with 60% coverage | missing events filled with their own mean |

::: {.note .note-plum}
Coverage is imputed with the submission's own mean, computed before filling. You
cannot improve your rank by predicting only the easy events.
:::

## Train Versus Test {.compare}

You never saw these returns. Neither did the model that made the prediction.

# What Carried It

## The Coefficient Table

::: {.lead}
Ridge on standardised signals. This is the slide worth arguing about.
:::

```
    capital_return  0.0458
guidance_magnitude  0.0361
 guidance_revision  0.0304
 demand_commentary  0.0271
  margin_direction  0.0221
  revenue_momentum  0.0164
management_hedging  0.0147
         mix_shift -0.0043
one_off_dependence -0.0023
```

::: {.note}
From my run on a different period. Yours will differ, and the differences are
the discussion.
:::

## Questions for the Table {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Which survived?]{.card-title}

A dimension that matters in May and vanishes in August was probably never real.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Which are the same thing?]{.card-title}

`guidance_revision` and `guidance_magnitude` are close to collinear. Ridge
splits them; the split is arbitrary.
:::

::: {.card}
[What is missing?]{.card-title}

Anything the ten facts never mention, your signals cannot see.
:::
:::

## Where the Bodies Are Buried

::: {.steps}
1. Ten dimensions, tuned by hand against a training number you looked at many times
2. One month, one market regime
3. No standard errors on any coefficient
4. Small caps with violent reactions dominate the tails
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Every one of these is a reason your held-out number is lower than your training
number. None of them is a reason to stop.
:::

# What This Is Not

## Explaining Is Not Predicting {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
We explained a return using information released at the same time as the return.
That is comprehension, not a trade.
:::

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[20%]{.stat-value}
[R-squared in the paper]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[0%]{.stat-value}
[of it is alpha]{.stat-label}
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
To trade this you would need the signal before the market has it. The call is
public the moment it ends.
:::

## What Would Make It a Strategy {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Speed]{.card-title}

Have the number before the price does. Minutes, and against everyone else doing
the same thing.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Drift]{.card-title}

Predict the days *after* the reaction, not the day of it. Post-earnings
announcement drift is a real and long-documented effect.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
The second one uses everything you built today and changes only the label.
Thursday we go there.
:::

## The Transferable Part

::: {.steps}
1. The model turns text into a number; conventional code decides what it means
2. The expensive step is shared; you differentiate on the cheap one
3. Signals are formed without the outcome, enforced by the imports
4. A positive R-squared is a hypothesis until a permutation test survives it
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
None of that is about earnings calls. It is how you build anything that reads
text and takes a position.
:::
